newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Senate approves tax rise package.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Senate approves tax rise package.

text.p: Argentina's Senate passed into law late on Wednesday Economy Minister Roque Fernandez's new package of tax increases, which was approved by the lower house of Congress last week.

The main points include a 46 percent rise in the tax on diesel, a 12 percent increase in the gasoline tax and tax hikes on natural gas and diesel vehicles. Income tax will rise to 33 percent from 30 percent for companies and high earners.
The bill also authorises the government to increase indebtedness this year by $4.0 billion.
The bill was passed by the ruling Peronist Party's large majority in the Senate and provincial party allies. It was opposed by the Radical Party.

Fernandez originally hoped the package would boost the budget by $1.2 billion this year to help head off a deficit he warned could be as high as $6.6 billion. But it has since been watered down at committee stages in Congress.

Earlier Wednesday the lower house of Congress voted into law a parallel bill allowing the central government to keep all revenues from the fuel hike, estimated at $1.6 billion annually. In exchange the provinces, who are usually given a share of fuel taxes, will get a share of personal wealth tax.
The Argentine Senate also voted on a law that would slap a 14 percent tax on food vouchers and eliminate family allowance benefits for workers earning more than $1,500 a month.

However, the bill, already approved by deputies, must return to the lower house since senators introduced a change raising the ceiling to $1,800 a month for workers in "hardship" provinces in the far north and south of the country.

Senators are confident these changes will be accepted by lower house. In the original proposal by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, the benefit was to be scrapped for all workers earning more than $1,000 a month.

The Peronist government's fiscal austerity drive has sparked protest from Argentine trade unions, who are staging their second general strike in two months on Thursday. They plan to demand more pro-growth policies to combat high unemployment of 17.1 percent.
